tagline: Entry-level project foundations across predictive, agile, and business analysis.

domains.name: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
domains.description: Core project life cycles, planning, roles and responsibilities, and common problem-solving tools.

domains.name: Predictive, Plan-Based Methodologies
domains.description: When and how to apply predictive, plan-based approaches and their project management plan components.

domains.name: Agile Frameworks/Methodologies
domains.description: When and how to apply adaptive approaches, plan iterations, and execute task management.

domains.name: Business Analysis Frameworks
domains.description: Business analysis roles, stakeholder communication, requirements, and product roadmaps.

questions.stem: How does a project differ from ongoing operations?

options.text: A project is a temporary endeavor undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result
A project repeats the same activities indefinitely to sustain a business
A project never has a defined end date
A project always produces an identical deliverable each time it runs

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** PMI defines a project as a temporary endeavor undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result; "temporary" means it has a definite beginning and end, and "unique" distinguishes it from repetitive work. Why the others are wrong: **B** describes ongoing operations, which are repetitive and sustaining; **C** every project is temporary and has an end, so this is the opposite of the definition; **D** producing identical output each time describes operational, not project, work.

questions.stem: Which life cycle is characterized by completing the scope, schedule, and cost planning up front and then executing against that fixed baseline?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A predictive, plan-based life cycle defines scope, schedule, and cost early and then manages change against those baselines, making it suitable for well-understood, stable requirements. Why the others are wrong: **A** adaptive life cycles welcome change and plan in short cycles rather than fixing scope up front; **C** incremental delivers the product in successive usable pieces rather than planning everything once; **D** iterative refines a deliverable through repeated cycles and does not rely on a fixed up-front baseline.

questions.stem: A team plans and delivers the product in short cycles, inspecting the result and adapting the plan after each cycle as requirements emerge. Which life cycle does this describe?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Planning and delivering in short cycles while inspecting and adapting as requirements emerge is the defining behavior of an adaptive (agile) life cycle. Why the others are wrong: **B** a predictive life cycle fixes scope, schedule, and cost up front rather than letting requirements emerge; **A** waterfall is a sequential predictive approach with little mid-stream adaptation; **D** a phase-gate life cycle uses formal gate reviews between phases and is typically predictive, not iterative adaptation.

questions.stem: Which document formally authorizes the existence of a project and gives the project manager authority to apply organizational resources?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The project charter is issued by the sponsor; it formally authorizes the project and grants the project manager authority to apply organizational resources to project activities. Why the others are wrong: **B** the project management plan describes how the project is executed and controlled but does not authorize it; **C** the scope statement details deliverables and boundaries, not authorization; **D** the WBS decomposes deliverables into work packages and is created after the project is authorized.

questions.stem: On a predictive project, what is the primary purpose of decomposing deliverables into a work breakdown structure (WBS)?

options.text: To list the project's risks in order of priority
To subdivide project deliverables into smaller, more manageable components down to the work-package level
To record lessons learned at the end of the project
To sequence activities and calculate the critical path

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The WBS is a deliverable-oriented hierarchical decomposition that subdivides the project scope into smaller, more manageable components, with the lowest level being the work package. Why the others are wrong: **A** prioritizing risks belongs to the risk register and qualitative analysis, not the WBS; **C** lessons learned are captured in a separate register, not the WBS; **D** sequencing and the critical path come from schedule network analysis, which uses the WBS-derived activities but is a different process.

questions.stem: In a project schedule, what does a milestone represent?

options.text: The longest activity on the critical path
A task that consumes the most resources
A significant point or event with zero duration
A buffer added to protect the project end date

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A milestone marks a significant point or event in the project — such as a phase completion or a key approval — and has zero duration because it represents a moment, not work. Why the others are wrong: **B** a resource-heavy task still has duration and is not a milestone; **A** the longest critical-path activity is an activity with duration, not a milestone; **D** a schedule buffer or reserve protects dates but is not the definition of a milestone.

questions.stem: Activity B cannot start until Activity A finishes. What type of logical dependency relationship is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** In a finish-to-start relationship, the successor (B) cannot begin until the predecessor (A) is complete; it is the most commonly used dependency in scheduling. Why the others are wrong: **A** start-to-start means the successor cannot start until the predecessor starts; **C** finish-to-finish means the successor cannot finish until the predecessor finishes; **D** start-to-finish means the successor cannot finish until the predecessor starts, a rare relationship.

questions.stem: A successor activity can begin only after a mandatory 3-day curing period follows its predecessor's completion. How should this delay be modeled in the schedule?

options.text: As 3 days of schedule reserve at the end of the project
As a lead of 3 days on the relationship
As a separate 3-day activity with its own resources
As a lag of 3 days on a finish-to-start relationship

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A lag is an imposed waiting time between activities; a mandatory curing period after the predecessor finishes is modeled as a lag on the finish-to-start link. Why the others are wrong: **B** a lead accelerates the successor (lets it start early) — the opposite of a required wait; **C** curing is passive elapsed time, not work needing resources, so a separate activity overstates effort; **A** schedule reserve covers risk and is held at the project or phase level, not used to model a known, required delay.

questions.stem: A project manager facilitates a meeting where the team generates as many ideas as possible without judging them, then organizes the ideas afterward. Which technique is being used?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Brainstorming generates a large quantity of ideas from a group while deferring judgment, after which the ideas are grouped and evaluated. Why the others are wrong: **A** multicriteria decision analysis scores options against weighted criteria to choose among them, not to generate ideas; **C** root cause analysis traces a problem to its underlying causes; **D** cost-benefit analysis compares expected costs against benefits to justify a choice.

questions.stem: Recurring defects appear in a deliverable. The team repeatedly asks "why" to trace each symptom back to its underlying source. Which problem-solving tool is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Asking "why" repeatedly to move from a symptom to its underlying cause is root cause analysis, commonly applied via the 5 Whys or an Ishikawa (fishbone) diagram. Why the others are wrong: **B** a RACI/responsibility assignment matrix maps people to activities, not causes; **C** a burndown chart tracks remaining work over time; **A** a stakeholder register lists and analyzes stakeholders, unrelated to defect causation.

questions.stem: Which role is accountable for providing the project's funding and championing it at the executive level?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The sponsor provides financial resources, champions the project to senior leadership, issues the charter, and helps remove high-level obstacles. Why the others are wrong: **B** the project manager leads day-to-day delivery but does not fund the project; **C** team members perform the work to create deliverables; **D** a functional manager oversees a department and supplies resources but is not the project's funding champion.

questions.stem: In a strong matrix organization, where does the project manager's authority generally stand relative to the functional manager's?

options.text: The project manager has moderate to high authority
The project manager has little to no authority
The project manager has no role; only functional managers exist
The project manager reports directly to each team member

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** In a strong matrix the balance of power favors the project manager, who holds moderate-to-high authority and often works full time, while functional managers still own their departments. Why the others are wrong: **B** little-to-no authority describes a weak matrix or functional structure; **C** functional-only structures are not matrices at all; **D** team members do not supervise the project manager in any standard structure.

questions.stem: A project has activities with durations: Start → A (4 days) → C (5 days) → End, and Start → B (6 days) → C. All links are finish-to-start. What is the project's critical path duration?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** C depends on both A and B, so it can start only after the later predecessor. Path A→C = 4+5 = 9 days; path B→C = 6+5 = 11 days. The longest (critical) path is 11 days. Why the others are wrong: **B** 9 days is the shorter A→C path, not the longest; **A** 6 days ignores activity C entirely; **D** A and B run in parallel, so their durations are not summed.

questions.stem: Which two characteristics are typical of a predictive (plan-based) life cycle? (Select two.)

options.text: Scope, schedule, and cost are defined early and managed against baselines
Detailed planning is done once at the start for the whole project
Requirements are expected to emerge and change continuously
Work is delivered in short timeboxed increments with frequent re-prioritization

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A predictive life cycle defines scope, schedule, and cost up front, manages them against baselines, and relies on detailed planning performed early (though predictive projects may still refine plans through rolling-wave planning as work proceeds). Why the others are wrong: **C** continuously emerging requirements describe an adaptive approach; **D** short timeboxed increments with frequent re-prioritization is a hallmark of agile/adaptive delivery, not predictive.

questions.stem: Which two items are commonly found in a project charter? (Select two.)

options.text: The assigned project manager and their authority level
Detailed activity-level cost estimates for every work package
The complete risk response plan for all identified risks

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A charter captures a high-level description and project boundaries plus the name of the assigned project manager and their authority. Why the others are wrong: **C** detailed work-package cost estimates are produced later during planning, not in the charter; **D** a complete risk response plan is developed during risk planning, well after the charter is issued.

questions.stem: Arrange the five PMI Process Groups in their typical logical order of emphasis across a project.
questions.explanation: The correct order is Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring and Controlling, then Closing. A project is first authorized in Initiating, then the approach is defined in Planning, the work is carried out in Executing, performance is measured and corrected in Monitoring and Controlling (which overlaps execution throughout), and the project or phase is formally finished in Closing. The order is right because you cannot plan before a project is authorized, cannot execute without a plan, and cannot close before the work and its control are complete.

questions.stem: Which situation most strongly favors choosing a predictive, plan-based approach?

options.text: Requirements are clear, stable, and well understood from the outset
Requirements are highly uncertain and expected to change frequently
The customer wants to inspect a working increment every two weeks
The team must experiment to discover what the customer actually needs

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Predictive approaches work best when requirements are clear, stable, and well understood, so the team can plan scope, schedule, and cost up front with confidence. Why the others are wrong: **B** high uncertainty and frequent change favor an adaptive approach; **C** wanting frequent working increments points to agile delivery; **D** experimenting to discover needs is exploratory work suited to adaptive methods.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of a scope baseline on a predictive project?

options.text: To list the names and contact details of all stakeholders
To serve as the approved reference against which scope performance is measured and changes are controlled
To record the order in which activities will be executed
To define how the team will communicate during the project

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The scope baseline — the approved scope statement, WBS, and WBS dictionary — is the reference used to measure scope performance and to control changes through integrated change control. Why the others are wrong: **A** stakeholder names belong in the stakeholder register; **C** activity order is the schedule's domain, not the scope baseline; **D** communication methods are documented in the communications management plan.

questions.stem: On a predictive project, a stakeholder requests a change that would expand the product scope. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Refuse the change because the scope baseline is fixed
Implement the change immediately to keep the stakeholder happy
Submit the request as a change request through the integrated change control process
Quietly absorb the extra work without documenting it

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Any change to an approved baseline must be submitted as a documented change request and evaluated through integrated change control before action is taken. Why the others are wrong: **B** acting without analysis or approval is uncontrolled scope creep; **A** a flat refusal is wrong because approved changes are allowed; **D** absorbing work undocumented (gold plating/scope creep) undermines the baseline and controls.

questions.stem: At a status review, a predictive project shows Earned Value (EV) = 80,000 and Actual Cost (AC) = 100,000. What does this indicate about cost performance?

options.text: The project is exactly on budget
The project is under budget for the work completed
The project is ahead of schedule
The project is over budget for the work completed (cost variance is negative)

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Cost variance = EV − AC = 80,000 − 100,000 = −20,000; a negative CV (and a CPI of 0.8, below 1.0) means the project has spent more than the value of work completed, so it is over budget. Why the others are wrong: **B** under budget would require EV greater than AC; **C** schedule status depends on EV versus planned value, not AC; **A** on budget would require EV to equal AC.

questions.stem: Which artifact decomposes the project's deliverables into a hierarchy of progressively smaller components ending in work packages?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The WBS is a deliverable-oriented hierarchical decomposition of the total project scope, with work packages at the lowest level. Why the others are wrong: **B** the risk register catalogs risks and responses; **A** the stakeholder engagement plan describes strategies to engage stakeholders; **D** the milestone list identifies key schedule events but does not decompose deliverables.

questions.stem: A predictive project's costs are tracked over time and plotted as a cumulative curve to show planned spending. What is this time-phased budget called?

options.text: Cost baseline (often shown as an S-curve)

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The cost baseline is the approved, time-phased budget used to measure and monitor cost performance; plotting cumulative cost over time typically produces an S-curve. Why the others are wrong: **B** a burndown chart shows remaining work in an iteration, used in agile; **C** a Pareto chart ranks causes by frequency; **A** a responsibility assignment matrix maps people to activities.

questions.stem: Which two documents together with the scope statement form the scope baseline on a predictive project? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The scope baseline consists of the approved project scope statement, the WBS, and the WBS dictionary. Why the others are wrong: **C** the issue log tracks issues during execution and is not part of any baseline; **D** the communications management plan is a subsidiary plan about information distribution, not a scope component.

questions.stem: Which subsidiary plan defines how project scope will be defined, validated, and controlled?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The scope management plan is a component of the project management plan that describes how scope will be defined, developed, monitored, controlled, and validated. Why the others are wrong: **B** the schedule management plan governs developing and controlling the schedule; **C** the cost management plan governs estimating, budgeting, and controlling costs; **A** the procurement management plan governs acquiring goods and services from outside the project.

questions.stem: In Scrum, who is accountable for ordering the product backlog to maximize the value the team delivers?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing value by managing and ordering the product backlog so the most valuable items are addressed first. Why the others are wrong: **B** the Scrum Master coaches the team and removes impediments but does not own backlog priority; **C** developers decide how to build items, not the business priority order; **D** the sponsor funds the effort but does not manage the backlog.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of the daily scrum (daily stand-up)?

options.text: For the Scrum Master to assign tasks to each developer
For developers to inspect progress toward the sprint goal and adapt their plan for the day
To demonstrate the completed increment to stakeholders
To re-estimate the entire product backlog

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The daily scrum is a short event for developers to inspect progress toward the sprint goal and adapt the plan for the next day's work. Why the others are wrong: **A** the self-managing team selects its own work; the Scrum Master does not assign tasks; **C** demonstrating the increment happens at the sprint review; **D** re-estimating the whole backlog is refinement work, not the daily scrum's purpose.

questions.stem: An agile team holds an event at the end of each sprint to reflect on how they worked and to identify improvements for the next sprint. Which event is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The sprint retrospective is the event where the team inspects its process, interactions, and tools, and plans improvements for the next sprint. Why the others are wrong: **B** the sprint review inspects the product increment with stakeholders, not the team's process; **A** sprint planning defines what and how work will be done in the upcoming sprint; **D** the daily scrum is a brief daily synchronization, not an end-of-sprint reflection.

questions.stem: A team limits the number of items allowed in each workflow column on a visual board to expose bottlenecks and improve flow. Which practice are they applying?

options.text: Limiting work in progress (WIP) on a Kanban board

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Setting work-in-progress limits per column is a core Kanban practice; it caps concurrent work, surfaces bottlenecks, and smooths flow. Why the others are wrong: **B** timeboxing fixes the length of an iteration but does not cap items per column; **C** a retrospective improves process through reflection, not WIP limits; **A** the critical path is a predictive scheduling concept, unrelated to Kanban flow.

questions.stem: On an agile project, which chart shows the amount of work remaining in a sprint trending down toward zero over time?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A burndown chart plots remaining work against time, ideally trending down to zero by the end of the sprint, helping the team track whether it will meet the sprint goal. Why the others are wrong: **B** a Gantt chart shows scheduled activities along a timeline in predictive planning; **C** a control chart monitors process stability against limits; **A** a network diagram shows activity dependencies and sequencing.

questions.stem: A backlog item is worth high business value but is technically easy and low effort. Using value-versus-effort prioritization, how should it be treated?

options.text: Always sequence it last regardless of value
Defer it because low-effort items add little value
Prioritize it early as a quick win

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** High-value, low-effort items are quick wins and should be pulled forward to deliver value early and cheaply. Why the others are wrong: **B** low effort does not mean low value — here the value is high, so deferring wastes an easy win; **C** discarding a valuable item is clearly wrong; **A** sequencing it last ignores its high value-to-effort ratio.

questions.stem: In the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe), what is an Agile Release Train (ART)?

options.text: A single Scrum team of seven developers
A long-lived team of agile teams that plans, commits, and delivers value together on a cadence
A document listing every requirement for a release
A tool for drawing the project's critical path

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** In SAFe, an Agile Release Train is a long-lived team of agile teams (a team of teams) that plans, commits, and delivers value together on a common cadence, typically a program increment. Why the others are wrong: **A** a single Scrum team is one team, not a team of teams; **C** a requirements list is an artifact, not an organizational construct; **D** critical-path tooling is a predictive scheduling concept, unrelated to ARTs.

questions.stem: According to the Agile Manifesto's values, which two are valued more highly? (Select two.)

options.text: Responding to change over following a plan
Processes and tools over individuals and interactions

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The Agile Manifesto values working software over comprehensive documentation and responding to change over following a plan. Why the others are wrong: **C** reverses the value — the Manifesto favors customer collaboration over contract negotiation; **D** reverses the value — it favors individuals and interactions over processes and tools.

questions.stem: Order the following Scrum events as they occur within and around a single sprint, from first to last.
questions.explanation: The correct order is sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review, then sprint retrospective. A sprint begins with sprint planning to set the goal and select work; the daily scrum recurs each day during the sprint to inspect and adapt; near the end the sprint review inspects the increment with stakeholders; and finally the retrospective reflects on how to improve. This order is right because planning must open the sprint, the daily scrum happens throughout execution, and the review (product) precedes the retrospective (process) that closes the sprint.

questions.stem: Which activity is a core responsibility of a business analyst on a project?

options.text: Authorizing the project and committing its funding
Removing impediments for the development team

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The business analyst focuses on eliciting, analyzing, documenting, and managing requirements so the right solution is built to meet stakeholder needs. Why the others are wrong: **B** authorizing the project and funding it is the sponsor's role; **C** removing impediments for the team is a Scrum Master responsibility; **D** approving vendor payments is a procurement/financial authority, not a BA task.

questions.stem: Gathering requirements directly from stakeholders through conversations, workshops, and observation is best described as which activity?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Elicitation is the act of drawing out information and requirements from stakeholders using techniques such as interviews, workshops, and observation. Why the others are wrong: **B** validation confirms the delivered solution meets the requirements and stakeholder needs; **C** traceability links requirements to their origins and deliverables; **D** prioritization ranks requirements by importance, not gathers them.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of a requirements traceability matrix?

options.text: To record the project's daily expenses
To link each requirement to its origin and track it through to the deliverables that satisfy it
To schedule the sequence of sprints
To list the project's communication channels

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A requirements traceability matrix links each requirement to its source and forward to the design, build, test, and deliverables that satisfy it, ensuring nothing is lost and scope stays controlled. Why the others are wrong: **A** daily expenses are tracked in cost/financial records; **C** sprint sequencing is a release/iteration planning concern; **D** communication channels are documented in the communications plan.

questions.stem: Which artifact provides a high-level, time-oriented view of how a product is expected to evolve and deliver value over upcoming releases?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A product roadmap is a high-level, time-oriented plan showing how a product will evolve and deliver value across upcoming releases, aligning stakeholders on direction. Why the others are wrong: **B** a sprint backlog is the detailed work selected for one sprint, not a long-range product view; **A** an issue log tracks issues needing resolution; **D** a change log records the status of change requests.

questions.stem: In an adaptive project, which artifact primarily holds the ordered list of features and requirements the team will work from?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** On adaptive projects, requirements are commonly captured and ordered in a product backlog (often as user stories), which the team draws from each iteration. Why the others are wrong: **B** the business case justifies the investment but is not the working requirements list; **C** the charter authorizes the project; **A** the traceability matrix links requirements to deliverables but is not the primary backlog of work in adaptive delivery.

questions.stem: How does the chosen project methodology influence how a business analyst handles requirements?

options.text: Adaptive projects require all requirements fully specified before any work begins
Requirements are handled identically regardless of methodology
Predictive projects favor detailed requirements documented up front, while adaptive projects favor requirements that emerge and are refined over iterations

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Methodology shapes BA practice: predictive projects emphasize detailed, baselined requirements defined up front, whereas adaptive projects let requirements emerge and be progressively elaborated across iterations. Why the others are wrong: **B** the approach clearly changes how and when requirements are detailed; **A** adaptive projects deliberately avoid fully specifying everything up front; **D** predictive projects rely heavily on documented requirements, not discourage them.

questions.stem: Which technique confirms that delivered functionality actually meets the agreed requirements and stakeholder needs before it is accepted?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Acceptance criteria define the conditions a deliverable must satisfy, and acceptance testing verifies the solution meets those criteria and stakeholder needs before acceptance. Why the others are wrong: **B** brainstorming generates ideas, it does not validate delivery; **C** resource leveling adjusts resource assignments on the schedule; **A** schedule compression (crashing/fast tracking) shortens duration, unrelated to validating requirements.

questions.stem: A business analyst must engage a stakeholder group with high power but low current interest in the project. What is the most appropriate engagement strategy?

options.text: Treat them the same as low-power, low-interest stakeholders
Ignore them because their interest is low
Flood them with every detailed status report and meeting invite
Keep them satisfied with focused, periodic communication appropriate to their influence

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** On a power/interest grid, high-power/low-interest stakeholders should be kept satisfied — engaged with the right level of focused communication so their influence stays supportive without overwhelming them. Why the others are wrong: **B** ignoring high-power stakeholders is risky because they can derail the project; **C** flooding them with detail can annoy and disengage them; **A** low-power/low-interest stakeholders are merely monitored, which under-serves a high-power group.

questions.stem: Which document identifies stakeholders and records information such as their interests, influence, and engagement needs?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The stakeholder register records identified stakeholders along with assessment information such as their interests, influence, expectations, and engagement needs. Why the others are wrong: **B** the risk register catalogs risks, not stakeholders; **C** the WBS decomposes deliverables; **D** quality metrics define measurable quality attributes, unrelated to stakeholder identification.

questions.stem: Which two are common requirements elicitation techniques a business analyst might use? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Facilitated workshops and interviews are classic elicitation techniques used to draw out requirements from stakeholders. Why the others are wrong: **C** earned value analysis measures cost and schedule performance, not requirements gathering; **D** critical path calculation is a scheduling technique, unrelated to eliciting requirements.

questions.stem: A business analyst is writing a user story. Which two elements are most essential to a well-formed user story? (Select two.)

options.text: A statement of who wants it, what they want, and why (the value)
Acceptance criteria that define when it is done
The exact number of code lines required

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A good user story states the role, the need, and the benefit ("As a… I want… so that…") and is paired with acceptance criteria that define when it is complete. Why the others are wrong: **C** a line-of-code count is an implementation detail, not part of a user story; **D** an invoice number is a procurement record with no place in a user story.

questions.stem: During iterative delivery, a stakeholder reviews a completed increment and realizes a previously approved requirement no longer reflects the real business need. What should the business analyst do?

options.text: Capture the feedback, reassess the requirement, and update/re-prioritize the backlog accordingly
Refuse to change anything because the requirement was already approved
Quietly delete the increment and hide the issue from stakeholders
Stop all delivery until a full predictive re-baseline is completed

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Validating requirements through delivered increments is exactly how adaptive work surfaces change; the BA captures the feedback, reassesses the requirement, and updates and re-prioritizes the backlog to reflect the true need. Why the others are wrong: **B** refusing change defeats the purpose of iterative feedback; **C** hiding the issue is unethical and harms the product; **D** halting everything for a heavy predictive re-baseline contradicts the adaptive approach in use.

questions.stem: A large construction project is organized so that a formal review decides whether the project may proceed from design into build. What is this review point called?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A phase gate is a review held at the end of a phase to decide whether to continue, change, or end the project before committing to the next phase. Why the others are wrong: **B** the daily scrum is a brief agile synchronization, not a go/no-go decision point; **A** a retrospective reflects on team process at a sprint's end; **D** a work package is the lowest level of the WBS, a unit of work rather than a decision review.

questions.stem: A new estimator prepares a cost estimate for a task by using the actual cost of a similar task from a past project and adjusting it for size. Which estimating technique is being used?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Analogous estimating uses values (such as cost or duration) from a similar past activity or project as the basis for the new estimate, adjusting for known differences. Why the others are wrong: **A** parametric estimating multiplies a unit rate by a quantity using a statistical relationship; **C** bottom-up estimating aggregates detailed estimates of the lowest-level components; **D** three-point estimating averages optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic values to account for uncertainty.

questions.stem: An activity has an optimistic estimate of 4 days, a most likely estimate of 6 days, and a pessimistic estimate of 14 days. Using the PERT (beta) formula, what is the expected duration?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The PERT beta formula is (O + 4M + P) / 6 = (4 + 24 + 14) / 6 = 42 / 6 = 7 days. Why the others are wrong: **A** 6 days is only the most likely value and ignores the optimistic and pessimistic ends; **C** 8 days would result from mis-weighting the most likely estimate; **D** 24 days is just the 4M term before dividing by 6.

questions.stem: During planning, the team records "the test environment will be available by week 3" as something believed true but not yet confirmed. How should this be classified?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** An assumption is a factor considered to be true, real, or certain for planning purposes without proof; if it turns out false it can become a risk or an issue. Why the others are wrong: **A** a constraint is a limiting factor that restricts options (for example a fixed deadline or budget), not a belief; **C** a milestone is a significant zero-duration event; **B** a deliverable is a tangible, verifiable output of the work.

questions.stem: A project manager adapts the organization's standard processes, choosing only the tools, techniques, and life-cycle elements that fit this specific project. What is this practice called?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Tailoring is deliberately selecting and adjusting the processes, methods, and life cycle to suit the project's context, size, and complexity. Why the others are wrong: **B** gold plating is adding unrequested extras beyond scope; **C** progressive elaboration is refining detail as more is known over time; **D** fast tracking is a schedule-compression technique that overlaps activities normally done in sequence.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes the project management plan from project documents such as the risk register or issue log?

options.text: They are identical and the terms are interchangeable
Project documents are approved baselines, while the project management plan is updated freely without control
The project management plan describes how the project is executed and controlled, while project documents are working records used to manage the project
The project management plan lists daily issues, while project documents define the baselines

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The project management plan defines how the work will be planned, executed, monitored, and closed (including baselines and subsidiary plans), whereas project documents like the risk register and issue log are operational records used while managing the project. Why the others are wrong: **B** reverses the relationship — the plan holds the controlled baselines; **A** they are distinct categories of outputs; **D** also reverses their roles, since issues are tracked in a project document, not the plan.

questions.stem: At the start of execution, the team and key stakeholders meet to confirm objectives, roles, and how they will work together. Which meeting is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A kickoff meeting brings the team and stakeholders together to align on objectives, scope, roles, and ways of working as execution begins. Why the others are wrong: **A** a lessons-learned review captures what went well or poorly, typically later or at closure; **C** a change control board evaluates change requests; **D** a sprint review demonstrates a completed increment to stakeholders in Scrum.

questions.stem: A team sorts a large set of brainstormed ideas into natural groupings based on their similarities to make sense of them. Which technique is being used?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** An affinity diagram organizes a large number of ideas into groups based on their natural relationships, making them easier to review and analyze. Why the others are wrong: **B** a Pareto chart ranks causes by frequency to find the vital few; **C** a control chart tracks whether a process is stable over time; **D** a scatter diagram shows the relationship between two variables.

questions.stem: Which chart displays scheduled activities as horizontal bars along a timeline, making start and finish dates easy to read?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A Gantt (bar) chart shows activities as horizontal bars positioned along a calendar timeline, with bar length representing duration. Why the others are wrong: **B** a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram maps potential causes of a problem; **C** a histogram shows the frequency distribution of data; **A** a RACI chart maps responsibilities of people to activities, not a timeline.

questions.stem: A scheduling tool reports that an activity has 4 days of total float. What does this mean?

options.text: The activity is on the critical path
The activity must start 4 days earlier than planned
The activity can be delayed up to 4 days without delaying the project finish date
The activity will take 4 extra days of effort

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Total float is the amount of time an activity can be delayed from its early start without delaying the project's finish date. Why the others are wrong: **B** float is permissible slack, not a requirement to start earlier; **A** critical-path activities have zero total float, so positive float means it is not critical; **D** float measures schedule flexibility, not additional work effort.

questions.stem: An agile team faces a decision and the facilitator asks each member to show a fist (zero) up to five fingers to gauge support before proceeding. Which decision technique is this?

options.text: Fist of five (fist to five) voting

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Fist of five is a quick group decision and consensus-gauging technique where members raise zero to five fingers to signal their level of support. Why the others are wrong: **B** multicriteria decision analysis scores options against weighted criteria on paper; **C** the critical path method calculates the longest schedule path; **D** Monte Carlo simulation models uncertainty by running many probabilistic iterations.

questions.stem: Which option best describes a deliverable?

options.text: A limiting factor that restricts the project team's options
Any unique and verifiable product, result, or capability to perform a service produced to complete a process, phase, or project
A factor assumed to be true for planning purposes
A list of stakeholders and their interests

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A deliverable is any unique, verifiable product, result, or service capability that must be produced to complete a process, phase, or project. Why the others are wrong: **A** describes a constraint; **C** describes an assumption; **D** describes the contents of a stakeholder register, none of which is the definition of a deliverable.

questions.stem: Which two inputs are the most direct components of the three-point (PERT) estimate for an activity's duration? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Three-point (PERT) estimating combines the optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic durations; the optimistic and pessimistic values are two of those three direct inputs. Why the others are wrong: **C** actual cost to date is an earned-value input, not part of a duration estimate; **D** the number of stakeholders does not feed the three-point duration formula.

questions.stem: Place the steps of a basic structured problem-solving approach in their correct order, from first to last.

options.text: Implement the solution and verify it worked

questions.explanation: The correct order is define the problem, identify the root cause(s), generate and select a solution, then implement and verify. You must understand and frame the problem before investigating why it occurs; only after the underlying cause is known can a sound solution be chosen; and finally the chosen solution is implemented and checked to confirm the problem is actually resolved. Jumping to solutions before defining the problem or finding its cause typically treats symptoms rather than the real issue.

questions.stem: A predictive project is behind schedule. The manager adds resources to a critical-path activity to shorten its duration, accepting higher cost. Which schedule-compression technique is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Crashing shortens duration by adding resources (such as overtime or extra staff) to critical activities, usually increasing cost. Why the others are wrong: **B** fast tracking overlaps activities normally done in sequence, adding risk rather than cost; **C** resource leveling adjusts start dates to balance resource demand and can lengthen the schedule; **A** rolling wave planning is a progressive-detailing technique, not a compression method.

questions.stem: At a checkpoint, a predictive project reports Planned Value (PV) = 50,000 and Earned Value (EV) = 45,000. What does the schedule variance indicate?

options.text: The project is ahead of schedule
The project is behind schedule (schedule variance is negative)
The project is exactly on schedule

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Schedule variance = EV − PV = 45,000 − 50,000 = −5,000; a negative SV (and an SPI of 0.9) means less value has been earned than planned, so the project is behind schedule. Why the others are wrong: **A** ahead of schedule would require EV greater than PV; **C** on schedule would require EV to equal PV; **D** budget status is judged by EV versus actual cost (CV), not by PV.

questions.stem: On a predictive project, which document records identified risks along with their analysis, owners, and planned responses?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The risk register is the artifact that captures identified risks, their assessment (probability and impact), assigned owners, and agreed response strategies. Why the others are wrong: **B** the milestone list records key schedule events; **C** the cost baseline is the time-phased budget; **D** the stakeholder register lists stakeholders and their interests, not risks.

questions.stem: A risk is identified that, if it occurs, would severely delay a predictive project, and it cannot be eliminated. The team buys insurance and hires a specialist subcontractor to handle it. Which risk response strategy is this for a threat?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Transferring a threat shifts the impact and ownership of the response to a third party, for example through insurance or subcontracting, while the risk itself still exists. Why the others are wrong: **B** avoiding eliminates the threat or its cause, which is stated to be impossible here; **A** accepting takes no proactive action; **D** exploit is a response for an opportunity, not a threat.

questions.stem: Which output of the Sequence Activities process visually shows project activities and the logical relationships (dependencies) among them?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A schedule network diagram is a graphical representation of the project's activities and the logical dependencies (relationships) between them. Why the others are wrong: **B** a responsibility assignment matrix maps people to activities; **C** a quality checklist verifies that required steps are performed; **A** a procurement statement of work describes goods or services to be purchased.

questions.stem: Which artifact maps project roles to activities using designations such as Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A RACI chart is a type of responsibility assignment matrix that links activities to roles using the labels Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed to clarify who does what. Why the others are wrong: **B** a burndown chart tracks remaining work over time; **A** a Pareto chart ranks causes by frequency; **D** the cost baseline is the time-phased budget, none of which assigns responsibilities.

questions.stem: Which two are valid response strategies for a negative risk (threat) on a predictive project? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Mitigate (reduce probability or impact) and avoid (eliminate the threat or its cause) are both threat response strategies, along with transfer and accept. Why the others are wrong: **C** enhance is an opportunity strategy that increases the chance or impact of a positive risk; **D** exploit is also an opportunity strategy aimed at ensuring a positive risk occurs.

questions.stem: In Scrum, what is the maximum length of a sprint?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A sprint is timeboxed to one month or less; shorter sprints generate more learning cycles and limit risk to a smaller window of cost and effort. Why the others are wrong: **A** one day is too short to deliver a usable increment and is not the defined limit; **C** three months exceeds the one-month maximum and reduces feedback frequency; **D** sprints are explicitly timeboxed, so there is a limit.

questions.stem: An agile team agrees on a shared checklist of conditions every backlog item must meet to be considered complete and potentially releasable. What is this called?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Definition of Done is a shared, agreed set of criteria a work item must satisfy to be considered complete and potentially shippable, ensuring consistent quality. Why the others are wrong: **B** the sprint goal is the single objective for one sprint, not a completion checklist; **C** the product vision describes the long-term aim of the product; **D** velocity is the amount of work a team completes per sprint, a metric rather than a quality standard.

questions.stem: A team estimates backlog items using relative sizes such as 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, and 13 by holding up cards and discussing differences. Which estimating technique is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Planning poker is a consensus-based, relative estimating technique where team members reveal cards (often Fibonacci-like story points) and discuss differences until they converge. Why the others are wrong: **B** bottom-up estimating sums detailed cost or duration figures, not relative sizes; **C** earned value analysis measures performance against a baseline; **A** the critical chain method schedules work around resource constraints and buffers.

questions.stem: An agile team uses a chart that plots cumulative work in each workflow state over time to visualize flow, throughput, and where work piles up. Which chart is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A cumulative flow diagram shows the amount of work in each state (e.g., to do, in progress, done) over time, helping a team spot bottlenecks, work-in-progress buildup, and throughput trends. Why the others are wrong: **B** a Gantt chart shows scheduled activity bars on a predictive timeline; **A** a network diagram shows activity dependencies; **D** a responsibility assignment matrix maps roles to tasks.

questions.stem: Which Extreme Programming (XP) practice has two developers working together at one workstation, one writing code while the other reviews each line as it is typed?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Pair programming is the XP practice in which two developers share one workstation, continuously reviewing the code as it is written to improve quality and spread knowledge. Why the others are wrong: **B** continuous integration merges and tests code frequently in a shared build; **C** test-driven development writes a failing test before the code that makes it pass; **D** refactoring improves the internal structure of code without changing its external behavior.

questions.stem: A product owner ranks backlog items by sorting them into Must have, Should have, Could have, and Won't have this time. Which prioritization method is being used?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** MoSCoW prioritizes requirements into Must have, Should have, Could have, and Won't have (this time), clarifying what is essential versus optional for a release. Why the others are wrong: **B** the critical path method is a predictive scheduling technique; **C** earned value management measures cost and schedule performance; **A** Pareto analysis ranks causes by frequency, not requirements by negotiated priority.

questions.stem: Which two are among the twelve principles behind the Agile Manifesto? (Select two.)

options.text: Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months
Welcome changing requirements, even late in development
Lock the scope at the start and resist all change
Measure progress primarily by the volume of documentation produced

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Two of the twelve agile principles are delivering working software frequently and welcoming changing requirements even late in development to give the customer a competitive advantage. Why the others are wrong: **C** contradicts the principle of welcoming change; **D** contradicts the principle that working software is the primary measure of progress, not documentation volume.

questions.stem: In Scrum, what is the sprint backlog?

options.text: The complete, ordered list of everything that might ever be needed in the product
The set of product backlog items selected for the sprint plus a plan for delivering them and the sprint goal
A long-range, time-based view of product releases
A record of impediments raised during the sprint

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The sprint backlog is the developers' plan: the product backlog items selected for the sprint, the plan to deliver them, and the sprint goal. Why the others are wrong: **A** describes the product backlog, the full ordered list for the product; **C** describes a product roadmap; **D** describes an impediment log, not the sprint backlog.

questions.stem: A business analyst classifies a need as a business requirement, a stakeholder requirement, or a solution requirement. Which of these describes the higher-level goals and objectives of the organization?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Business requirements describe the higher-level needs of the organization as a whole, such as the goals, objectives, and reasons the project is undertaken. Why the others are wrong: **B** solution requirements describe the features and functions the solution must have; **A** transition requirements describe temporary capabilities needed to move from the current to the future state; **D** quality requirements are a type of non-functional requirement, not the organization's overarching goals.

questions.stem: A business analyst distinguishes between what the solution must do and how well it must perform. A requirement that the system respond within two seconds is best classified as which type?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A response-time target describes a quality attribute (performance) rather than a behavior, making it a non-functional requirement. Why the others are wrong: **B** a functional requirement specifies what the system must do (a behavior or feature); **C** a business requirement states an organizational goal; **A** a transition requirement covers temporary capabilities needed to move to the new solution, such as data migration or training.

questions.stem: After elicitation, a business analyst restates the captured requirements back to stakeholders and reconciles conflicting inputs to ensure a shared, consistent understanding. Which activity is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Confirming elicitation results means reviewing the gathered information with stakeholders, resolving conflicts, and ensuring the requirements are recorded accurately and consistently. Why the others are wrong: **B** prioritizing ranks requirements by importance, not for accuracy; **C** decomposing the WBS breaks deliverables into work packages on predictive scope work; **D** calculating earned value measures project performance, unrelated to confirming requirements.

questions.stem: A business analyst draws a diagram showing the steps a user takes and the system responses to complete a goal, including the main flow and alternative flows. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A use case or process flow models the interactions between actors and the system to achieve a goal, capturing the main flow and alternatives to clarify requirements. Why the others are wrong: **A** earned value analysis measures cost and schedule performance; **C** Monte Carlo simulation models risk through repeated probabilistic runs; **D** critical path analysis identifies the longest path in a schedule network.

questions.stem: Which group of stakeholders does a business analyst most directly serve by ensuring the right requirements are defined and met?

options.text: Only the external auditors of the company
The business stakeholders and end users whose needs the solution must satisfy

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The business analyst works on behalf of the business stakeholders and end users to ensure the solution's requirements reflect and satisfy their real needs. Why the others are wrong: **B** auditors may be stakeholders but are not the primary group whose needs drive requirements; **A** vendors supply goods or services and are not the central beneficiaries of requirements work; **D** regulators impose constraints but are not the main stakeholders the BA represents.

questions.stem: Two stakeholders disagree about a requirement's priority, and the conflict is blocking the backlog. What is the most appropriate first action for the business analyst?

options.text: Implement both requirements at full priority regardless of capacity
Pick the requirement preferred by the louder stakeholder
Drop both requirements to avoid the conflict
Facilitate a discussion to understand each interest and reach a resolution, escalating to the decision authority only if needed

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The BA should facilitate dialogue to surface each stakeholder's underlying interest and drive toward a shared resolution, escalating to the proper decision authority only if consensus cannot be reached. Why the others are wrong: **B** deciding by who is loudest ignores value and good facilitation; **C** dropping valid requirements discards business value; **A** forcing both at full priority ignores capacity and defeats prioritization.

questions.stem: A product owner wants a single, easy-to-read view that communicates the product's direction and goals to leadership without committing to exact dates. Which artifact best fits?

options.text: A product roadmap organized by goals or themes
A detailed Gantt chart of every task

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A goal- or theme-based product roadmap communicates direction and intended outcomes at a high level, aligning leadership without locking in precise dates. Why the others are wrong: **B** a detailed Gantt chart commits to specific dated tasks, the opposite of what is wanted; **C** a traceability matrix links requirements to deliverables for control, not strategic direction; **D** an earned value report measures cost and schedule performance, not product direction.

questions.stem: On an adaptive project, how is requirements detail typically handled compared with a predictive project?

options.text: All requirements are fully detailed and frozen before any development starts
Requirements are progressively elaborated, with detail added just in time before the work is done
Requirements are never written down in any form
Only the project sponsor may define any requirement

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Adaptive projects use progressive elaboration, detailing backlog items just in time (for example, refining a story shortly before a sprint) rather than specifying everything up front. Why the others are wrong: **A** describes the predictive approach, not adaptive; **C** adaptive teams still capture requirements, often as user stories and acceptance criteria; **D** the product owner orders the backlog, but requirements come from many stakeholders, not the sponsor alone.

questions.stem: A delivered increment passes its tests but a key stakeholder says it does not actually solve their business problem. Which distinction does this best illustrate?

options.text: Validation only checks spelling and formatting
Verification and validation mean the same thing
Verification confirms the solution was built right; validation confirms the right solution was built
Verification is performed only by the sponsor

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Verification checks that the product meets its specifications (built right), while validation confirms it meets the stakeholder's actual need (the right product); passing tests yet missing the need is a validation gap. Why the others are wrong: **B** the two terms are distinct; **A** validation is about meeting real needs, far beyond spelling; **D** verification is a quality activity for the team, not exclusively the sponsor's task.

questions.stem: Which two characteristics describe a good (well-formed) requirement? (Select two.)

options.text: Written so that only its author can interpret it
Intentionally vague so it can mean many things

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Quality requirements are unambiguous (clearly understood the same way by all readers) and testable/verifiable (you can confirm whether they are met). Why the others are wrong: **C** a requirement interpretable by only one person fails the clarity and shared-understanding test; **D** deliberate vagueness invites scope disputes and cannot be verified.

questions.stem: Which two activities are central to conducting effective stakeholder communication as a business analyst? (Select two.)

options.text: Tailoring the message and format to each stakeholder's needs and influence
Actively listening and confirming understanding through feedback
Sending the same dense technical report to everyone regardless of audience
Withholding information from stakeholders to retain control

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Effective communication means tailoring the message and channel to each audience and listening actively while confirming that the message was understood. Why the others are wrong: **C** one-size-fits-all dense reports ignore audience needs and reduce comprehension; **D** withholding information erodes trust and undermines stakeholder engagement.

questions.stem: An organization establishes a department that defines project management standards, provides templates, and offers coaching but lets each project manager retain control of their own project. What type of project management office (PMO) is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A supportive PMO plays a consultative role, supplying templates, best practices, training, and lessons learned while exercising a low degree of control. Why the others are wrong: **B** a controlling PMO requires compliance with frameworks and has a moderate degree of control; **C** a directive PMO takes over and directly manages the projects, the highest degree of control; **D** "virtual PMO" is not one of PMI's three standard PMO types.

questions.stem: A program manager oversees several related projects that are managed in a coordinated way to obtain benefits not available from managing them individually. What is this grouping called?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A program is a group of related projects managed in a coordinated way to obtain benefits and control not available from managing them individually. Why the others are wrong: **A** a portfolio is a collection of projects, programs, and operations grouped to meet strategic objectives, and its components are not necessarily related; **B** a phase is a stage within a single project's life cycle; **C** a work package is the lowest level of a WBS.

questions.stem: While defining a project, the team labels the company's existing approval policies and its risk-tolerance culture as influences on the project. In PMI terms, these are best classified as which input?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Enterprise environmental factors (EEFs) are conditions not under the team's immediate control that influence the project, such as organizational culture, risk tolerance, and governance structures. Why the others are wrong: **A** organizational process assets are the company's reusable plans, processes, templates, and historical records, not its culture; **B** work performance data are raw observations gathered during execution; **D** a change request is a formal proposal to modify a document or baseline.

questions.stem: A project manager wants to reuse a prior project's templates, the lessons-learned repository, and a standardized change-control procedure. Which input do these represent?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Organizational process assets (OPAs) are the plans, processes, policies, templates, and knowledge bases (including historical information and lessons learned) specific to the organization that the team can draw on. Why the others are wrong: **A** enterprise environmental factors are external/internal conditions like culture or market, not reusable assets; **C** a milestone list records key schedule events; **D** a risk-adjusted backlog is an agile prioritization concept, not a source of templates.

questions.stem: A project team plans only the immediate upcoming work in detail and leaves work far in the future at a high level, adding detail as the project progresses. Which planning technique is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Rolling wave planning is an iterative technique in which near-term work is planned in detail while work further out is planned at a higher level and elaborated as it approaches. Why the others are wrong: **A** critical chain scheduling builds the schedule around resource constraints and buffers; **B** Monte Carlo simulation models uncertainty through many probabilistic runs; **C** earned value management measures performance against a baseline, not how planning detail is staged.

questions.stem: A scheduler computes early start and early finish dates by working through the network diagram from the project start toward the end. Which calculation is being performed?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The forward pass moves through the network from start to finish to calculate the early start and early finish of each activity. Why the others are wrong: **A** the backward pass works from the end back to the start to compute late start and late finish; **C** resource smoothing adjusts activities within their float to avoid exceeding resource limits; **D** variance at completion is an earned-value forecast, not a network calculation.

questions.stem: Two activities must occur in sequence because of the physical nature of the work: concrete must be poured before it can be finished. What kind of dependency is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A mandatory (hard logic) dependency is inherent in the nature of the work or required by contract, like pouring concrete before finishing it. Why the others are wrong: **A** a discretionary (soft logic) dependency is based on preference or best practice and could be reordered; **B** an external dependency involves factors outside the project, such as a regulator or supplier; **D** an internal resource dependency reflects team or equipment availability, not the physical nature of the work.

questions.stem: A project manager wants to discover a stakeholder's true position by meeting one-on-one and asking open and follow-up questions. Which data-gathering technique is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** An interview is a direct, often one-on-one conversation using prepared and spontaneous questions to draw out detailed information from an individual. Why the others are wrong: **A** a questionnaire/survey collects information from many respondents through written questions; **B** a focus group convenes pre-qualified participants in a moderated group discussion; **C** benchmarking compares practices or metrics against a reference to identify improvements.

questions.stem: A project shows activities Start → A (3) → B (5) → End and Start → C (2) → B. All links are finish-to-start. How much total float does activity C have?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** B starts only after both A (3) and C (2) finish, so B waits on the later predecessor, A, at day 3. A's path drives B, so C can slip from finishing at day 2 to day 3 without delaying B; total float = 3 − 2 = 1 day. Why the others are wrong: **A** zero float would mean C is critical, but path A (3) is longer than path C (2); **C** 2 days overstates the slack and equals C's duration, not its float; **D** 3 days confuses A's duration with C's float.

questions.stem: A project manager states that meeting the schedule deadline is the top priority, then cost, then scope, and documents how these will be balanced when conflicts arise. Which set of factors is being managed?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, and risk are competing project constraints; changing one usually affects the others, so the manager prioritizes how trade-offs will be balanced. Why the others are wrong: **A** communications channels describe information flow among stakeholders; **C** organizational process assets are the company's reusable processes and records; **D** procurement thresholds set authority limits for purchasing, none of which is the prioritized constraint set.

questions.stem: Which document captures detailed information about a single project activity, such as its scope of work, responsible party, and resource requirements?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Activity attributes extend the activity list with details such as predecessors, successors, resource requirements, constraints, and the person responsible, supporting schedule development. Why the others are wrong: **B** the stakeholder register lists stakeholders and their interests; **C** the business case justifies the investment in the project; **D** the quality policy states the organization's overall intentions regarding quality, not activity-level detail.

questions.stem: Which two are typical responsibilities of the project manager (rather than the sponsor or team)? (Select two.)

options.text: Developing the project management plan and integrating its components
Leading the team and managing day-to-day project work and communications
Providing the project's funding and the business justification
Performing the hands-on technical work to build each deliverable

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The project manager develops and integrates the project management plan and leads the team while managing the day-to-day work, stakeholders, and communications. Why the others are wrong: **C** providing funding and the business justification is the sponsor's responsibility; **D** producing the hands-on deliverables is the work of team members, not the project manager.

questions.stem: Which two statements about milestones are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: A milestone can mark the start or end of a phase or a major deliverable
A milestone consumes resources just like a normal activity
A milestone is always the longest activity on the critical path

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A milestone is a significant point or event with zero duration, and it can mark the beginning or completion of a phase, a key approval, or a major deliverable. Why the others are wrong: **C** milestones represent moments, not work, so they consume no resources; **D** a milestone is not an activity at all, so it cannot be the longest activity on the critical path.

questions.stem: Place these schedule-development steps in the order they are typically performed, from first to last.

options.text: Define the activities from the work packages
Sequence the activities and set dependencies
Develop the schedule (model and baseline it)

questions.explanation: The correct order is define the activities, sequence them, estimate their durations, then develop the schedule. You first break work packages into specific activities; only then can you arrange those activities in logical order with their dependencies; durations are estimated once the activities and their relationships are known; and finally the activities, sequence, durations, and resources are combined into the schedule model that is baselined. Estimating before the activities exist, or building the schedule before sequencing and durations are set, would skip required inputs.

questions.stem: On a predictive project, a status report shows Cost Performance Index (CPI) = 1.10. What does this value indicate?

options.text: The project is earning $1.10 of value for every $1.00 spent (under budget)
The project is spending $1.10 for every $1.00 of value earned (over budget)
The project is exactly on budget

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** CPI = EV / AC; a CPI of 1.10 means the project earns $1.10 of value for each $1.00 spent, so it is performing under (better than) budget. Why the others are wrong: **B** describes a CPI below 1.0 (over budget); **C** on budget would be a CPI of exactly 1.0; **D** schedule status is read from the SPI, not the CPI.

questions.stem: A predictive project has a Budget at Completion (BAC) of 200,000 and a current CPI of 0.80. Assuming current performance continues, what is the Estimate at Completion (EAC)?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** When current performance is expected to continue, EAC = BAC / CPI = 200,000 / 0.80 = 250,000. Why the others are wrong: **A** 160,000 multiplies BAC by CPI instead of dividing; **B** 200,000 is the original BAC, which ignores the unfavorable performance; **D** 280,000 does not follow from any standard EAC formula with these inputs.

questions.stem: After deliverables are completed and verified, the customer formally signs off that they meet acceptance criteria. Which predictive process produces this formal acceptance?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Validate Scope is the process of formalizing acceptance of the completed project deliverables by the customer or sponsor, producing accepted deliverables. Why the others are wrong: **A** Control Quality inspects deliverables for correctness and produces verified deliverables that feed Validate Scope, but it is about correctness, not customer sign-off; **C** Define Scope creates the scope statement; **D** Sequence Activities arranges activities in logical order.

questions.stem: A predictive project applies a defined amount of money or time set aside for the "known unknowns" — identified risks with planned responses. What is this reserve called?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A contingency reserve covers identified risks (known unknowns) and is part of the cost baseline, controlled by the project manager. Why the others are wrong: **A** management reserve is held for unforeseen work (unknown unknowns), sits outside the cost baseline, and needs management approval to use; **C** the cost baseline is the approved time-phased budget that includes contingency reserves; **D** profit margin is a commercial markup, not a risk reserve.

questions.stem: Which artifact lists the products, services, or results to be purchased from outside the project and describes them in enough detail for sellers to determine if they can provide them?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A procurement statement of work describes the items to be acquired in sufficient detail for prospective sellers to determine whether they can supply them. Why the others are wrong: **B** the lessons-learned register records knowledge gained during the project; **C** a burndown chart tracks remaining work in an iteration; **D** a stakeholder engagement assessment matrix compares current versus desired engagement levels, none of which defines procurement scope.

questions.stem: A buyer wants the seller to bear most cost risk on a well-defined scope, agreeing on a single set price for the work. Which contract type best fits?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A firm-fixed-price contract sets one price for a well-defined scope, placing the greatest cost risk on the seller, who must deliver regardless of its actual costs. Why the others are wrong: **A** cost-plus-fixed-fee reimburses the seller's costs plus a fixed fee, putting cost risk on the buyer; **B** time and materials bills per hour and per unit, with open-ended cost risk for the buyer; **D** cost-plus-incentive-fee reimburses costs and shares savings or overruns, so the buyer still bears cost risk.

questions.stem: Which two outputs are produced by the Control Scope process on a predictive project? (Select two.)

options.text: Change requests when variances are found

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Control Scope monitors scope status against the baseline, producing work performance information (such as how scope is performing) and change requests when corrective or preventive action or variances require them. Why the others are wrong: **C** the project charter is an output of Develop Project Charter during initiating; **D** the product backlog is an adaptive artifact, not an output of predictive scope control.

questions.stem: An agile team measures the average number of story points it completes per sprint to forecast how much it can take on next. What is this metric called?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Velocity is the amount of work (often in story points) a team completes per iteration; its average is used to forecast future capacity. Why the others are wrong: **A** cycle time measures how long a single item takes from work-start to done; **B** lead time measures from request to delivery; **C** cost variance is an earned-value measure of budget performance, not throughput.

questions.stem: A Scrum team writes a short statement describing the single objective it intends to achieve during the upcoming sprint, giving the work coherence. What is this called?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The sprint goal is the single objective for the sprint; it provides focus and coherence, guiding the team while allowing flexibility in exactly which backlog items deliver it. Why the others are wrong: **A** the product vision describes the long-term aim of the entire product; **C** the definition of ready is the agreed criteria for a backlog item to be eligible for a sprint; **D** the release plan spans multiple sprints toward a release, not one sprint's objective.

questions.stem: An agile team and product owner periodically review upcoming backlog items, adding detail, splitting large items, and re-ordering them. This ongoing activity is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Product backlog refinement (grooming) is the ongoing activity of adding detail, estimates, and order to backlog items and breaking large items into smaller ones so they are ready for future sprints. Why the others are wrong: **A** the sprint review inspects the completed increment with stakeholders; **B** the daily scrum synchronizes the day's work toward the sprint goal; **D** a retrospective reflects on process improvement, not backlog preparation.

questions.stem: In SAFe, multiple agile teams on an Agile Release Train gather for a two-day cadence-based event to align on a shared set of objectives for the next several iterations. What is this event called?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** PI (Program Increment) planning is the cadence-based SAFe event where all teams on an Agile Release Train plan together and commit to a shared set of PI objectives for the upcoming increment. Why the others are wrong: **A** the daily scrum is a single team's brief daily sync; **C** the sprint retrospective reflects on one team's process at a sprint's end; **D** a change control board evaluates change requests, a predictive governance activity.

questions.stem: A team finds that an emerging requirement is unclear and risky, so it dedicates a short, time-boxed investigation to learn enough to estimate and plan it. What is this effort called?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A spike is a time-boxed research or prototyping activity used to reduce uncertainty so the team can better understand, estimate, or de-risk a backlog item. Why the others are wrong: **B** a milestone is a zero-duration significant event; **C** a change request is a formal proposal to alter a baseline, typical of predictive governance; **D** a work package is the lowest level of a WBS, not an investigative activity.

questions.stem: On a Scrum team, who is accountable for coaching the team in self-management, facilitating events, and helping remove impediments?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Scrum Master serves the team by coaching self-management, facilitating Scrum events, and helping remove impediments so the team can focus on delivering value.
